This manual provides a technical reference for gas plant automation systems, instrumentation, PLC hardware, HMI
applications, troubleshooting methods, process control, and safety fundamentals.
This manual is a controlled, living document. It is reviewed and updated as plant procedures evolve. Revision 1.2 converts the
earlier manual to reference-manual format, corrects technical errors identified in peer review, and adds standard ladder logic
patterns (see Appendix C). Do not distribute outside the facility without authorization.

Section 1: Gas Plant Process Flow Overview

1.1 Natural Gas Processing Plant Overview
A natural gas processing plant receives raw wellhead gas — a mixture of methane (CH₄), heavier hydrocarbons (ethane,
propane, butane, pentane+), water vapor, hydrogen sulfide (H₂S), carbon dioxide (CO₂), and trace contaminants — and
transforms it into pipeline-quality "sales gas" plus valuable liquid products. The processing train follows a predictable sequence
of unit operations, each with its own instrumentation, control loops, and safety systems.
This sequence is fundamental to automation maintenance and troubleshooting. Every control loop, HMI screen, alarm, and
interlock exists to serve a specific step in this chain. The six primary stages are summarized below.
Stage 1 — Inlet Separation
Raw wellhead gas enters the plant through inlet metering skids and flows into inlet separators (also called slug catchers on
wet-gas systems). These vessels use gravity, baffles, and sometimes coalescing elements to separate three phases: gas
(vapor), condensate (liquid hydrocarbons), and produced water. Key controlled variables are separator pressure and liquid
levels. A pressure control valve (PCV) regulates gas outlet pressure; level control valves (LCV) drain liquids to downstream
treating.
Stage 2 — Compression
After separation, the gas may need compression to raise it to pipeline or treating pressures. Reciprocating and centrifugal
compressors are common. Critical instrumented variables include suction/discharge pressures and temperatures, vibration (on
rotating equipment), lube-oil pressure, and surge control on centrifugal compressors. Anti-surge control loops and high-high
pressure shutdowns (PAHH) are essential safety functions here.
Stage 3 — Dehydration (Glycol)
Glycol dehydration removes water vapor to prevent hydrate formation and meet pipeline water dew-point specifications
(typically <7 lb H₂O/MMSCFD or <4°C dew point). Tri-ethylene glycol (TEG) absorbs water from the gas in a contactor
(absorber column) and is regenerated in a reboiler. Controlled variables include contactor pressure, reboiler temperature
(typically 195–205°C), and glycol circulation rate (flow control).
Stage 4 — Amine Treating (H₂S / CO₂ Removal)
Amine treating (also called sweetening) removes acid gases — primarily H₂S and CO₂ — using amine solvents (MEA, DEA,
MDEA, or blends). Gas contacts lean amine in an absorber; the rich amine is regenerated in a stripper (regenerator) column.
Pipeline specifications limit H₂S to ≤4 ppm and CO₂ to ≤2%. Analyzer transmitters (AT) continuously monitor treated gas H₂S
content. Critical controlled variables: absorber pressure, regenerator temperature (typically 115–125°C), lean amine flow rate,
and reboiler duty.
Stage 5 — NGL Fractionation
Natural Gas Liquids (NGL) fractionation separates the heavier hydrocarbon liquids (C2+) into marketable products: ethane,
propane, butane, and natural gasoline (pentane+). This is accomplished using a series of distillation columns (deethanizer,
depropanizer, debutanizer). Each column has precise temperature and pressure control profiles, with multiple tray or packed
sections. Product purity is monitored by analyzer transmitters (chromatographs or on-line BTU analyzers).
Stage 6 — Metering / Custody Transfer
Custody transfer metering measures the final sales-gas volume and energy content for commercial billing. Turbine meters,
ultrasonic meters, or orifice meters with AGA-7 or AGA-3 calculations are typical. These meters require high accuracy (±0.25%
or better), temperature/pressure compensation, and chromatograph integration for BTU content. Regulatory compliance
(FERC, RRC Texas) governs documentation requirements.

1.4 Safety Interlock Overview
Every stage of the gas plant is protected by a layered safety architecture. Technicians must understand three fundamental
safety device categories before working on any loop.

Emergency Shutdown (ESD)
An Emergency Shutdown (ESD) system is a dedicated logic solver (or SIS controller — see Section 9) that monitors critical
process variables (pressure, level, temperature, fire/gas) and, upon detecting an unsafe condition, drives the process to a safe
state by closing isolation valves, tripping compressors, and opening blowdown valves. ESD systems are independent of the
Basic Process Control System (BPCS/PLC). ESD logic is typically implemented as de-energize-to-trip (fail-safe) — the valve is
held open by power; loss of signal closes it.
Pressure Safety Valves (PSV)
A Pressure Safety Valve (PSV) is a purely mechanical last line of defense. It is set to open at or below the vessel Maximum
Allowable Working Pressure (MAWP) and relieves excess pressure directly to the flare system without any electronic signal.
Alarm and trip setpoints are ordered PAH < PAHH < PSV set pressure ≤ MAWP. PSVs require periodic testing and must never
be blocked in without proper isolation permits. A PSV is never defeated without authorization.

Section 2: Instrumentation Fundamentals

2.1 The 4–20 mA Signal Standard
The 4–20 mA current loop is the dominant analog signal standard in process control. It represents a process variable as a
proportional current: 4 mA = 0% of range (live zero), 20 mA = 100% of range. The signal is a current (not a voltage), which
makes it inherently immune to line resistance and EMI noise over long cable runs — both critical advantages in an outdoor gas
plant environment.
Why a "Live Zero" at 4 mA?
A healthy, powered transmitter outputs at least 4 mA even when the process is at its minimum value. If the signal drops below
3.6 mA, the DCS/PLC can detect it as a broken wire or transmitter power failure — a "below live zero" fault — and
annunciate an alarm. A signal of 0 mA unambiguously indicates an open circuit.
Signal Conversion Formula

 (* Convert mA signal to % of span *)
 Percent (%) = (mA - 4) / 16 × 100

 (* Convert % to engineering units *)
 EU Value = PV_Min + (Percent / 100) × (PV_Max - PV_Min)

 (* Combined single-step conversion *)
 EU Value = PV_Min + ((mA - 4) / 16) × (PV_Max - PV_Min)

 (* Reverse: EU to expected mA output *)
 mA = ((EU Value - PV_Min) / (PV_Max - PV_Min)) × 16 + 4

 (* Example: PT range 0–300 PSIG, reading 12 mA *)
 EU = 0 + ((12 - 4) / 16) × (300 - 0) = 0.5 × 300 = 150 PSIG

2.3 HART Protocol Basics
HART (Highway Addressable Remote Transducer) is a bi-directional digital communication protocol superimposed on the
standard 4–20 mA signal. It uses frequency-shift keying (FSK) to transmit digital data at 1,200 baud without disturbing the
analog signal.
  • Primary Variable (PV): The main measurement — represented by the 4–20 mA signal and also transmitted digitally.
     Example: process pressure in PSIG.
  • Secondary Variable (SV): A secondary measurement transmitted digitally only. Example: sensor temperature on a
     pressure transmitter.
  • Tertiary / Quaternary Variables (TV, QV): Additional digital variables on multivariable transmitters (e.g., temperature-
     compensated flow from a multivariable DP transmitter).
  • Polling Address: Each HART device has a polling address: 0–15 for HART 5 devices and 0–63 for HART 6/7 devices. In
     point-to-point mode (the most common), the polling address is 0 and the 4–20 mA analog signal is active. In multidrop
     mode, the analog signal is fixed (typically 4 mA) and devices use non-zero addresses.
  • HART Communicator: A handheld device (e.g., Emerson 475 or AMS Trex) that connects across the loop (at the
     terminals or at the barrier) to read/write configuration, trim the instrument, run diagnostics, and perform calibration.
 NOTE — HART in the Field
 Connect the HART communicator across a loop resistance of 230–600 Ω (typically 250 Ω), either at the instrument
 terminals or at the field junction box, not at the PLC card terminals. If total loop resistance is below 230 Ω, the HART
 communicator will not establish communication; add a HART resistor.

2.4 Instrument Calibration

Zero and Span
Zero is the adjustment that sets the transmitter's output to exactly 4.000 mA at the Lower Range Value (LRV — 0% of input
range). Span is the adjustment that sets the output to exactly 20.000 mA at the Upper Range Value (URV — 100% of input
range). Always adjust zero first, then span, then re-check zero (they can interact).
5-Point Calibration Procedure
A 5-point calibration verifies transmitter accuracy across five input values: 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of span. For an
upscale check (ascending) and a downscale check (descending), this produces 10 data points — sufficient to detect
hysteresis and linearity errors.

2.5 Loop Check Procedure (Step-by-Step)
A loop check verifies that a complete instrument loop — from field sensor through wiring, junction box, cable, IS barrier, PLC
AI card, to HMI display — functions correctly before commissioning or after maintenance.
 1. Obtain authorization. Confirm MOC or loop check work order. Notify the control room operator that the loop is being
      tested and may produce false readings or alarms — request alarm suppression if needed.
 2. Gather documentation. Retrieve the loop drawing, P&ID, instrument datasheet, and calibration record for the instrument
      under test.
 3. Inspect field wiring. At the field instrument, check terminal connections are tight, wire labels match the loop drawing, no
      corrosion or moisture intrusion, and cable gland is sealed.
 4. Measure loop current at field instrument. Connect a calibrated milliammeter (or use the HART communicator's mA
      measurement function) in series with the loop. Verify minimum current (≥3.6 mA) is present — indicates loop is powered
      and complete.

5. Apply 0% input. Inject 4.000 mA using a precision mA source (loop calibrator, e.g., Beamex MC6 or Fluke 789). Confirm
      PLC AI card reads 0% of engineering units. Confirm HMI displays correct 0% value.
 6. Apply 25%, 50%, 75%, 100% inputs. For each point, confirm PLC and HMI values track the injected signal within
      acceptable tolerance (typically ±0.1% of span for most process instruments).
 7. Verify alarms. Inject a value above the PAH setpoint — confirm alarm annunciates on HMI with correct tag, description,
      and priority. Test PAHH if applicable.
 8. Check fail-safe behavior. Open the loop (disconnect one wire). Confirm the PLC flags bad quality through the channel
      under-range/fault status and that a bad-quality alarm annunciates on the HMI.
 9. Restore wiring. Reconnect all wires, verify connections are tight, replace covers and glands.
 10. Clear alarm suppression. Notify control room that loop check is complete and loop is returned to service. Confirm
      operator restores normal alarm state.
 11. Document results. Record all readings on the loop check form or calibration record. Note any deviations, corrective
      actions taken, and the as-left condition. Sign and date.

2.6 Intrinsic Safety Basics
Intrinsic Safety (IS) is a method of explosion protection for instruments in hazardous (classified) locations. It limits the
electrical energy (voltage, current, and capacitance/inductance) in the hazardous area circuit to levels incapable of igniting a
flammable atmosphere — even under fault conditions. IS circuits are approved for use in Class I, Div. 1 (or ATEX/IECEx Zone
0/1) hazardous locations.
Zener Barriers
A Zener barrier (or simply "barrier") is a passive IS device mounted in the safe area (control room). It contains Zener diodes
that clamp voltage to a safe level and resistors that limit fault current. Zener barriers require a certified intrinsically safe earth
bond (≤1Ω ground connection) to function correctly. They are simple and inexpensive but sensitive to ground quality.
Galvanic Isolators
A galvanic isolator provides IS protection using transformer or optical isolation — no ground bond required. It converts the
hazardous-area signal to the safe area with complete galvanic isolation. Galvanic isolators are preferred when ground loop
issues exist or when a reliable IS earth is not available. They are more expensive than Zener barriers but easier to install
correctly.

Redundancy: Primary / Secondary Controller
Redundancy in ControlLogix uses two identical chassis (primary and secondary) connected via 1756-RM2 modules and a
fiber optic crosslink cable. The primary controller is active (scanning, controlling); the secondary is in a synchronized warm-
standby state. The secondary receives periodic crossloads — transfers of the tag database, I/O image, and program state —
so it can take over with zero data loss. Switchover triggers include: CPU fault, power loss on primary, communication loss, or
user-commanded switchover. Switchover time is typically <100 ms for a warm-redundant system.

3.4 Networking
EtherNet/IP Overview
EtherNet/IP (Ethernet Industrial Protocol) is the Rockwell Automation standard network for ControlLogix communication. It
uses standard IEEE 802.3 Ethernet hardware and the CIP (Common Industrial Protocol) application layer. Two messaging
types are fundamental:
  • Implicit Messaging (I/O messaging): Real-time, cyclic data exchange between controller and I/O devices. The connection
     is established at startup and data is transferred automatically at the RPI rate. Used for: local and remote FLEX I/O data,
     drive I/O, safety I/O.
  • Explicit Messaging (MSG instruction): On-demand, request-response data exchange. The controller initiates a read or
     write to another device upon logic triggering. Used for: reading data from another PLC, writing recipe setpoints,
     communication with HMI OPC server, diagnostics.
Device Level Ring (DLR) Topology
A Device Level Ring (DLR) is a high-availability Ethernet topology in which devices are connected in a ring rather than a star.
The ring supervisor sends beacon frames (typically every 400 µs) to detect a cable break. On a fault, the ring supervisor
reconfigures the network to a linear topology within about 3 ms, restoring communication without a managed switch at every
node. DLR is common in FLEX I/O banks, VFD networks, and remote I/O panels.
CIP Basics
CIP (Common Industrial Protocol) is the application-layer protocol used by EtherNet/IP (and also DeviceNet and ControlNet). It
defines objects, services, and a consistent device model. Key CIP services used in plant work:
  • CIP Data Table Read/Write: Used in MSG instructions to read or write a specific tag in another controller by name.
  • CIP Generic: Used for manufacturer-specific operations, drive parameter reads, and module configuration.
  • Connected Explicit: Persistent connection for repeated MSG reads (more efficient than unconnected when polling
     frequently).

4.4 FLEX I/O Configuration in Studio 5000 (Step-by-Step)
 1. Open the project in Studio 5000. In the Controller Organizer, right-click I/O Configuration → New Module.
 2. Select the adapter module. Search for "1794-AENTR" and select it. Enter the adapter's IP address (e.g., 10.10.1.20),

      frequently the ControlLogix polls the entire FLEX bank. Typical value: 20 ms.

      module in slot order (Slot 1 = first I/O module after adapter, Slot 2 = second, etc.). Select the correct part number (e.g.,
      1794-IE8 for AI), configure its signal type (mA or voltage), and set any module-specific options (filter time for DI, fault

 CAUTION — Prescan, Power-Up, and Communications Loss
 Prescan runs on every Program-to-Run transition and power-up. During prescan:
   • OTE bits are cleared.
   • OTL/OTU bits keep their last value.
   • ONS storage bits are set (no first-scan pulse).
   • TON timers are reset; RTO status bits are cleared but .ACC is kept.
   • DINT and REAL values are kept.
 On HMI communications loss, HMI-written request bits stay at their last value. On MSG failure, destination data goes stale
 and keeps its last value. Clear HMI requests in logic after use (Pattern A1/A7) and gate MSG data on communications
 health (Snippet 8). Review the analog output fault and program-mode states for each loop.

Common Bad Actor Alarms and Suppression Strategies
  • Chattering alarms: Alarm activates and clears repeatedly within a short period (e.g., a level alarm oscillating ±2% around
     a setpoint). Solution: increase deadband, move setpoint further from normal operation, or add time delay filter.
  • Stale alarms: Alarm that has been active for days or weeks without operator action. Solution: shelve with expiry time,
     investigate root cause, redesign setpoint or process.
  • Nuisance alarms during startup/shutdown: Normal process transients exceed alarm limits during non-steady-state.
     Solution: implement state-based alarming (alarms active only in applicable operating mode).
  • Flood alarms: A single process upset triggers dozens of alarms simultaneously (consequence alarms). Solution:
     rationalize to first-out alarm design; use alarm suppression for downstream alarms when root cause is identified.

6.4 HMI Screen Design Guidelines
Navigation Hierarchy
Effective HMI navigation follows a four-level hierarchy that allows operators to quickly drill from a plant-wide overview to a
specific instrument detail without confusion:
 1. Level 1 — Plant Overview: Single-screen birds-eye view of all major process units with key KPIs (throughput, pressures,
      alarms). Always accessible from any screen.
 2. Level 2 — Area Overview: One screen per major process area (Separation, Compression, Dehydration, Amine,
      Fractionation, Metering). Shows all loops, equipment statuses, and active alarms in that area.
 3. Level 3 — Unit/Equipment: Detailed P&ID-style mimic for one unit (e.g., Inlet Separator). Shows all instruments with live
      values, control valve positions, motor statuses, and setpoints.
 4. Level 4 — Faceplate / Detail: Pop-up controller faceplate for a single loop — PV, SP, mode, output %, trend, alarm
      setpoints. Accessed by clicking on any instrument on a Level 3 screen.

Terminal Block Numbering Convention
Terminal blocks must be numbered sequentially with a logical, documented system. The recommended convention:
  • Format: [Panel ID]-TB[Group]-[Terminal Number] — example: MCC-1-TB2-14
  • Power distribution terminals: group TB1 (AC power), TB2 (24 VDC), TB3 (24 VDC common)
  • Analog signal terminals: group TB10–TB19 (one group per FLEX I/O bank or AI card)
  • Digital input terminals: group TB20–TB29
  • Digital output terminals: group TB30–TB39
  • IS barrier terminals: group TB50–TB59 — physically separated from all other terminals
  • Earth/ground terminals: group TBG (green terminal blocks, always grounded)
Cable Separation Rules
  • Minimum 12 inches (305 mm) of physical separation between signal cables (4–20 mA, discrete I/O, network) and power
     cables (480 VAC motor, VFD output, 120 VAC control power) for parallel runs exceeding 10 feet.
  • Where cable trays must cross, the crossing shall be at 90 degrees to minimize coupling.
  • VFD output cables (motor leads) are a strong source of EMI and must be in dedicated, separate conduit — never share
     conduit or tray with signal cables.
  • Never route analog signal cables through conduit shared with power cables, even if only passing through for a short
     distance.
Shield Grounding
  • Each shielded instrument cable must have its drain wire (shield) connected to the instrument signal ground bus in the
     control panel — one end only (panel end).
  • The field end of the shield must be left floating (not connected to the instrument housing, junction box, or conduit).
     Connecting both ends creates a ground loop, which introduces noise.
  • The instrument signal ground bus must be bonded to the main panel earth ground with a single, low-impedance
     connection.
  • IS circuit drain wires must connect to the IS earth bar — not the same bus as non-IS ground.

7.3 Grounding and Shielding Reference
  • Control Room Ground Bus: A bare copper or tinned copper bus bar runs the length of the control room cable tray,
     bonded to the building steel and the electrical system safety earth. All panel ground wires, cable shields, and IS earth bars
     bond to this bus.
  • Panel Bonding: Every metal panel, enclosure, cable tray section, and conduit run must be bonded to the plant ground grid
     with a minimum #6 AWG green insulated conductor. Jumper bonds (braided strap or #6 AWG) are required at cable tray
     joints where paint may interrupt conductivity.
  • EMI Mitigation for VFD Installations:
  • Install VFD in a metal enclosure with proper EMI gasket sealing.
  • Use shielded motor cable (VFD-rated cable, all three phases + shield + PE) from VFD output to motor; ground both ends of
     the shield for VFD motor cable.
  • Install output dV/dt filters or sine wave filters between VFD and motor if cable length exceeds 100 feet or if motor insulation
     is not inverter-rated.
  • Keep VFD input power wiring, VFD output (motor) wiring, and signal wiring in separate conduits and trays.
  • Do not run communication cables (Ethernet, DeviceNet) in the same conduit as VFD motor leads.

Section 8: Troubleshooting Guide

8.1 Systematic Troubleshooting Methodology
Effective troubleshooting is a disciplined, sequential process. Random probing wastes time, introduces new problems, and can
create safety incidents. Technicians should apply this 7-step process every time, regardless of urgency.
 1. Define the Problem: State clearly what is NOT working. "PV not reading" is vague. "SEP_PT_101 reads 0 PSIG on the
      HMI but the field pressure gauge reads 205 PSIG" is precise. A well-defined problem is half solved.
 2. Observe Symptoms: Gather all observable evidence before touching anything. Check: HMI tag quality, alarm history,
      PLC online diagnostics, fault LEDs on modules, related tags, when the problem started, what changed just before it
      started.
 3. Identify Possible Causes: Generate a list of all plausible causes based on symptoms. Use logic: if the problem is isolated
      to one tag, the cause is in that specific loop. If multiple loops on the same module are bad, the module or its power is
      suspect.
 4. Test Hypotheses (Least Invasive First): Start with checks that require no interaction with live equipment — visual
      inspection, software diagnostics, HMI configuration review. Then move to measurements that require minimal interaction
      (check voltage at terminals without disconnecting wires). Avoid disconnecting wires or removing modules until simpler
      checks are exhausted.
 5. Isolate the Fault: Using test results, narrow the fault to a specific component, cable segment, or software element.
      Example: signal is correct at field junction box but wrong at panel terminal → fault is in the cable between junction box
      and panel.
 6. Repair or Replace: Apply the correct fix. Do not bypass the root cause; address it directly. Obtain required permits
      (LOTO, hot work, entry) before physical work. Document the work performed.
 7. Verify and Document: Confirm normal operation is restored (loop check, HMI verification, alarm test). Complete the work
      order or maintenance record. Update the loop drawing if any wiring was changed. Notify the control room operator that
      the loop is back in service.

 WARNING — Before Any Troubleshooting
 LOTO (Lockout/Tagout): Isolate and de-energize equipment before touching live terminals or removing modules, unless
 procedures explicitly permit live maintenance and a JSA (Job Safety Analysis) has been completed. Never assume a circuit
 is de-energized; verify with a calibrated meter. In Class I, Division 1 areas, obtain a hot work permit before using any non-IS
 tools or equipment. When in doubt, consult the supervisor.

8.3 Quick Diagnostic Checklists

Checklist: When a Control Loop Won't Respond
 1. Verify the loop is NOT in bypass or maintenance mode — check bypass key switch and HMI status.
 2. Check PLC controller status — is it in RUN mode (not FAULT or PROGRAM mode)?
 3. Check I/O module status LEDs and Studio 5000 I/O tree — any faults on the AI or AO module?
 4. Verify the PID rung executes unconditionally in a periodic task and that .UPD equals the task period.
 5. Check PID mode: is .SWM (software manual) or .MO (operator manual) set? If so, the output is under manual control.
 6. Verify the process variable (PV) is valid: is the AI reading a realistic value, stuck at a limit, or flagged Bad?

7. Measure mA signal at the AI card terminals — does it match the expected process value?
 8. Go to the field instrument — does it have power? Is its local indicator reading correctly?
 9. For AO (output): measure mA at the AO card output terminals — is the PLC actually sending the commanded signal?
 10. Check the field actuator (control valve): is air supply present? Is positioner receiving the mA signal?
 11. Stroke the valve manually from the positioner — does it move freely? If not, call mechanical team.
 12. Check for any pending task overrun or program fault that may have halted the control routine.
 13. Review the PID tuning — is integral gain so high that the loop oscillates and appears unresponsive?
 14. Check for a latched BPCS trip (SEP_Trip_OK = 0) that may be overriding the control valve command.
 15. Review loop drawing for any manual bypass valves or isolation valves that may have been left closed.
Checklist: Before Calling the Engineer
 1. ☐ All fault LEDs, alarm messages, and error codes have been observed, recorded, and photographed where permitted.
 2. ☐ Exact tag names, module slot numbers, and I/O addresses involved have been noted.
 3. ☐ Alarm history and trends have been checked for when the problem first appeared.
 4. ☐ The problem has been confirmed NOT to be a normal process upset (check the P&ID, ask the operator).
 5. ☐ The most obvious causes (power, wiring, physical inspection) have been tested.
 6. ☐ Measurements (mA readings, voltage readings, LED states) have been documented.
 7. ☐ Changes to the system in the last 24 hours (maintenance, modifications, configuration changes) have been identified.
 8. ☐ The maintenance history (CMMS) has been checked for recent work on this loop or nearby equipment.
 9. ☐ Any corrective action attempted, and its result, has been documented.
 10. Is this issue affecting plant safety, production rate, or regulatory compliance? (Determines urgency of escalation.)
Checklist: After Any Control System Change (MOC / Post-Change Verification)
 1. Complete and close the Management of Change (MOC) form — get required signatures before going live.
 2. Download the project to the controller and verify no download errors or I/O module faults appear.
 3. Perform a loop check on all affected tags — verify field-to-HMI signal integrity (Section 2.5).
 4. Test all modified or new ladder logic rungs using forced I/O (with proper LOTO and operator awareness).
 5. Verify all alarm setpoints are correctly configured in both PLC and HMI.
 6. Test alarm annunciation — confirm alarms appear on HMI with correct priority, description, and audible annunciation.
 7. Test ESD and safety interlock logic if any changes were made — function test in accordance with proof test procedure.
 8. Verify PLC program backup has been saved to the project file server (not just to the controller flash).
 9. Update all affected loop drawings, I/O schedules, and cause and effect matrix to reflect the change.
 10. Notify all affected operators and document the change in the Control Room Logbook.
 11. Update the HMI tag list and historian configuration if new tags were added.
 12. Close out all work orders, permits (LOTO, hot work), and document "as-left" condition of all affected instruments.

Section 9: Safety and SIS Basics

9.1 Process Safety Fundamentals
HAZOP (Hazard and Operability Study)
A HAZOP is a structured, systematic review of a process design to identify potential hazards and operability problems. A
multidisciplinary team (process engineer, instrument engineer, operator, safety specialist, and often an independent facilitator)
reviews every process node using standardized guidewords applied to process parameters (flow, pressure, temperature,
composition, level).
 Guideword                   Meaning                                                    Example Applied to Flow
 No / None                   Complete negation of the design intent                     No flow when flow is required (blocked line, pump trip)
 More                        Quantitative increase above design                         More flow than expected (control valve fails open)
 Less                        Quantitative decrease below design                         Less flow than required (partial blockage, pump
                                                                                        degraded)
 Reverse                     Opposite direction from design intent                      Reverse flow (check valve failure, backpressure event)
 Other Than                  Complete substitution — wrong material, phase,             Liquid carry-over in gas stream (separator performance
                             or condition                                               failure)
 As Well As                  Additional (impurity or phase) present                     Water in product hydrocarbon (separator malfunction)
 Part Of                     Only part of the design intent is achieved                 Partial blockage in one branch of a multi-branch system

Layers of Protection Analysis (LOPA)
LOPA is a semi-quantitative method for evaluating whether existing and proposed protection layers provide sufficient risk
reduction for a specific accident scenario. The risk is evaluated against a company risk tolerance criterion (typically expressed
as a maximum acceptable frequency of a serious event — e.g., 1×10 ⁴ per year for a fatality).⁻
The layers of protection, from innermost to outermost, are:
 1. BPCS (Basic Process Control System): The PLC/DCS control system maintaining normal operating conditions. NOT an
      independent protection layer if it is also the initiating cause.
 2. Operator Alarm and Response: An alarm that an operator detects and acts upon within a required response time.
      Typically assigned a Probability of Failure on Demand (PFD) of 0.1 (1 in 10 chance of failure) per occurrence.
 3. Safety Instrumented System (SIS): An independent logic solver with dedicated sensors and final elements, designed per
      IEC 61511 using devices certified to IEC 61508 or justified by prior use. Provides the most reliable automated protection.
 4. Relief Devices (PSV, rupture disk): Mechanical devices requiring no logic — open automatically at set pressure. Highly
      reliable but require periodic testing.
 5. Physical Protection (Dikes, Blast Walls): Passive protection limiting consequences after a release. Does not prevent the
      event, only mitigates consequences.

IEC 61511 is the international standard for the functional safety lifecycle of Safety Instrumented Systems in the process

  • Phase 2: SIS design — architecture, technology selection, SIL verification

• Phase 3: Installation, commissioning, and validation testing
  • Phase 4: Operations and maintenance — proof tests, bypasses, management of change
  • Phase 5: Decommissioning

Proof Testing
A proof test is a periodic functional test of the entire SIF (sensor → logic solver → final element) to detect dangerous
undetected (DU) failures, which would prevent the SIF from responding on demand. The proof test interval (typically annual or

performed on a live process without a written proof test procedure, an authorized bypass in place, and communication with the
control room operator.

Natural gas (primarily methane, CH₄) is flammable within a specific concentration range in air:
  • LEL (Lower Explosive Limit): 5 vol% methane in air — below LEL, the mixture is too lean to ignite.
  • UEL (Upper Explosive Limit): 15 vol% methane in air — above UEL, the mixture is too rich to ignite (though it will ignite if
     diluted back into the flammable range).
  • Plant action levels: alarm at 10% LEL (0.5% methane); evacuate at 25% LEL (1.25% methane); hot work prohibited above
     10% LEL.
Fire and Gas (F&G) System
The Fire and Gas (F&G) system is an independent system that monitors the gas plant for flammable gas releases, toxic gas
(H₂S), smoke, heat, and flame. Key detector types:
  • Catalytic bead (pellistor) detector: Detects flammable gas by oxidation on a heated bead. Measures 0–100% LEL.
     Susceptible to poisoning (silicones, lead) and water flooding. Requires regular calibration (monthly or per manufacturer
     spec).
  • Infrared (IR) point detector: Detects hydrocarbon gas by infrared absorption. Immune to poisoning; functional in inert
     atmospheres; better choice for most gas plant applications. Also measures 0–100% LEL.
  • Flame detector: UV, IR, or UV/IR combination. Detects actual flame (fire). UV detectors are sensitive to welding arcs and
     sunlight — ensure proper positioning and arc flash suppression settings.
  • F&G voting logic: F&G system uses voting (e.g., 1oo2 or 2oo3 detectors per zone) before initiating emergency actions
     (ESD, deluge, PA system) to avoid spurious trips from a single faulty detector.

LOTO Procedure Summary
Lockout/Tagout (LOTO) is the OSHA-mandated procedure (29 CFR 1910.147) for controlling hazardous energy before
maintenance. Steps for electrical LOTO:
 1. Notify affected employees and operators.
 2. Identify all energy sources (electrical, pneumatic, hydraulic, process pressure/chemistry, gravity).
 3. Shut down the equipment using normal stopping procedure.
 4. Isolate each energy source at its isolation point (disconnect, valve, etc.).
 5. Apply the personal lock and tag to each isolation point.
 6. Release/restrain stored energy (bleed lines, block valves, vent pressure, support suspended loads).
 7. Verify isolation — test for zero energy state (use calibrated voltage tester, check pressure gauges).
 8. Perform work. Keep lock applied at all times.
 9. Remove tools; ensure no personnel are in the hazard zone.
 10. Remove lock and tag — only by the person who applied it.
 11. Restore energy; notify operator; confirm equipment is safe to operate.

Lab 1: Instrument Loop Check — Pressure Transmitter (Site Form Discipline)
Objective: Perform a complete loop check on a 4–20 mA pressure transmitter from field sensor through junction box, IS
barrier, and AI card to the HMI display, using the plant loop-check form and the work-control flow in Section 0.5. Use a
training-loop tag assigned by the supervisor; SEP-PT-101 is an example only.
Equipment / Tools: Calibrated loop calibrator (mA source/measure, e.g., Fluke 789), HART communicator (Emerson 475 or
Trex), calibrated digital multimeter, laptop with Studio 5000 (online), access to InTouch HMI, loop drawing, instrument
datasheet, loop check form.
Safety Precautions: Obtain loop check work order. Notify control room operator — request alarm suppression on affected
tags. Confirm area classification — use only IS tools in Class I Div 1 areas. Do not remove transmitter from process without
line breaking permit and LOTO.
Background Theory: A loop check verifies the electrical signal path from the field transmitter to the control system, confirming
that scaling, tag mapping, and alarm setpoints are correctly configured. Loop checks are required after installation, after any
wiring modification, and at defined intervals per the instrument maintenance plan. The 4–20 mA signal represents 0–100% of
the instrument's calibrated range.
Procedure
 1. Review the loop drawing. Identify transmitter tag (e.g., SEP-PT-101), range (0–300 PSIG), IS barrier type, AI card
      slot/channel, and HMI tag name.
 2. Notify the control room operator: "Performing loop check on SEP-PT-101. Expect artificial readings for approximately 30
      minutes. Please suppress alarms on this tag."
 3. At the field transmitter, remove the housing cover. Verify wiring matches the loop drawing. Check terminal block
      connections are tight.
 4. Connect the HART communicator across the transmitter loop terminals (or at the junction box). Read transmitter: model,
      serial number, configured range, current PV, and loop current. Record on loop check form.
 5. Using the loop calibrator in mA-source mode, disconnect the transmitter signal lead and inject 4.000 mA. At the control
      room/HMI, observe SEP-PT-101 reading — should display 0.0 PSIG (±0.5 PSIG acceptable).
 6. Inject 8.000 mA — HMI should read 75.0 PSIG.
 7. Inject 12.000 mA — HMI should read 150.0 PSIG.
 8. Inject 16.000 mA — HMI should read 225.0 PSIG.
 9. Inject 20.000 mA — HMI should read 300.0 PSIG.
 10. Inject a value above the PAH setpoint (example: PAH = 250 PSIG; inject 17.6 mA ≈ 255 PSIG). Confirm the PAH alarm
      annunciates on the HMI after the configured on-delay, with the correct tag, description, and priority.
 11. Open the loop (disconnect one wire). Confirm the channel under-range/fault status sets, the HMI shows bad quality, and
      a bad-quality alarm annunciates.
 12. Restore transmitter wiring. Re-read HART — confirm transmitter PV matches process (local gauge if available).
 13. Request operator to restore alarm suppression. Confirm tag is reading correctly on HMI.
 14. Complete and sign the loop check form. File per plant document control procedure.
Expected Results: All five injection points within ±0.5% of full span (±1.5 PSIG for a 300 PSIG span). Alarms trigger and clear
at configured setpoints. Fault alarm triggers on open loop.
Troubleshooting Tips: If the HMI reads a fixed value regardless of injection, check whether the AI tag is aliased to the wrong
channel. If HART will not communicate, verify 230–600 Ω loop resistance. If the alarm does not trigger, check the alarm
suppression status in InTouch.
Close-out: Record as-found mA and EU, as-left mA and EU, who was notified, alarm-suppression start/stop time, forces used
(must be none at the end), and supervisor initials. If the assigned tag is a SIF sensor, stop; that work is outside the technician
authorization envelope (Section 0.2).
Review Questions: Appendix F.2, Lab 1.

Lab 2: FLEX I/O Module Replacement (Hot-Swap)
Objective: Safely remove and replace a failed 1794-IE8 analog input module while the FLEX I/O bank remains powered,
without losing communication to other modules.
Equipment / Tools: Replacement 1794-IE8 module (same hardware rev as installed), flathead screwdriver, ESD wrist strap,
laptop with Studio 5000 online, MOC form, loop check form for re-verification.
Safety Precautions: Complete MOC form before proceeding. Notify operator that AI signals on this module (channels 0–7)
will go to fault/zero during replacement. Wear ESD wrist strap when handling module. Confirm replacement module is the
same catalog number and hardware revision. Do not remove terminal base — field wiring remains connected throughout.
Background Theory: FLEX I/O hot-swap separates the electronics module (which carries the circuitry) from the terminal base
(which carries the field wiring). Removing the module stops data exchange for that module only — the adapter and other
modules in the bank remain communicating. When the new module is inserted, the adapter automatically reconfigures it and
restores data exchange.
Procedure
 1. Complete and obtain approval for the MOC form. Document: affected tags, replacement module catalog number,
      estimated downtime, notification to operators.
 2. In Studio 5000, go online. Verify the 1794-AENTR adapter and other modules in the bank are in normal (green) status.
      Note which channels are active on the failed 1794-IE8.
 3. Notify the control room operator: "Replacing IE8 module in slot [X] of FLEX_SEP_01. Tags SEP_PT_101 through
      SEP_FT_101 will show fault values for approximately 2 minutes."
 4. Locate the 1794-IE8 in the bank. Observe the failed module's status LED (likely red or off).
 5. Press and hold the module release latch (orange tab on some versions; check product bulletin). Rock the module slightly
      and lift it vertically from the terminal base. The terminal base (with wiring) remains mounted.
 6. Inspect the terminal base connector pins — no damage or corrosion. Insert the new 1794-IE8 module into the terminal
      base: align the module body with the base, press down firmly until the latch clicks. The module status LED should flash
      green, then go solid green.
 7. In Studio 5000, observe the I/O tree — the replaced module should show normal (green) status within 10–30 seconds.
 8. Verify all AI tags on the replaced module are reading correct process values (not clamped at 0 or full scale, and not
      flagged Bad).
 9. Perform abbreviated loop checks on at least two channels: inject 12 mA (50%) and verify HMI reads correctly.
 10. Notify the control room operator: "Module replacement complete. All signals restored. Please verify SEP-PT-101 and
      associated tags."
 11. Document completion of MOC, record new module serial number, and update the instrument maintenance record.
Expected Results: Module replacement completed without loss of communication to other modules. All AI channels restored
to correct readings within 2 minutes. No new faults in controller.
Troubleshooting Tips: If module shows red after insertion — check for part number mismatch; may require module
configuration re-download. If one channel remains bad after replacement — fault is in field wiring or instrument, not module.
Review Questions: Appendix F.2, Lab 2.

Lab 3: Build a Motor Start/Stop Rung in Studio 5000
Objective: Create a motor start/stop rung with seal-in logic on a bench controller, create the required tags, download, and test
using bench inputs, including wire-break and mode-change behavior.
Equipment / Tools: Studio 5000 Logix Designer v36; 1769-L33ER bench controller at firmware v36 (or Studio 5000 Logix
Emulate); bench DI/DO simulator (NO momentary START switch, NC STOP, OL, and E-STOP switches, pilot light); laptop.
Safety Precautions: Bench controller or emulator only; never download to a production controller. Confirm the bench
controller is not connected to live process equipment. Clear all forces before ending the lab.
Background Theory: The motor start/stop with seal-in is the most fundamental discrete control circuit in industrial automation.
The seal-in (holding) contact is a contact of the output in parallel with the momentary start pushbutton; it keeps the circuit ON
after the start button is released. Only the stop circuit, a protective device, or a trip can break the seal-in. Health inputs follow
the fail-safe convention in Section 0.3.
Procedure
 1. Create a new Studio 5000 project for the 1769-L33ER at firmware v36 (or an Emulate controller). Use a project name that
      is visually distinct from production projects (Section 0.7).
 2. In the Controller Organizer, expand Tasks → MainTask → MainProgram. Right-click MainProgram → Add → New
      Routine. Name: "Motor_Control", Type: Ladder Diagram.
 3. Set the MainProgram properties: Main Routine = Motor_Control.

4. Wire the bench simulator per the bench drawing: START (NO momentary), STOP (NC), OL (NC), and E-STOP auxiliary
      (NC) to DI points; pilot light to a DO point.
 5. Create alias tags to the bench points: START_PB, STOP_OK (1 = stop not pressed and wire intact), OL_OK (1 = overload
      healthy), E_STOP_OK (1 = E-stop released), and Motor_Run (DO, pilot light).
 6. In Rung 0, enter the run rung in Neutral Text (rung block below).

 Rung 0 – Run with seal-in
 [XIC(START_PB) ,XIC(Motor_Run) ]XIC(E_STOP_OK)XIC(STOP_OK)XIC(OL_OK)OTE(Motor_Run);

 7. Add the rung comment: "Motor start/stop with seal-in. START_PB = NO momentary. STOP_OK, OL_OK, E_STOP_OK =
      NC health inputs (1 = healthy). Motor_Run = starter coil."
 8. Verify the routine (no errors) and save the project.
 9. Download to the bench controller and place it in Run mode.
 10. Press START: Motor_Run = 1 and the pilot light turns on.
 11. Release START: Motor_Run remains 1 (seal-in holding).
 12. Open STOP: Motor_Run = 0. Return STOP to normal: Motor_Run remains 0 until START is pressed again.
 13. Open the OL switch and press START: Motor_Run remains 0 while OL_OK = 0. Repeat with the E-STOP switch.
 14. Wire-break test: with the motor running, disconnect the STOP wire at the DI terminal. Motor_Run = 0 (fail-safe).
      Reconnect the wire.
 15. Mode-change test: with the motor running, switch the controller to Program and back to Run. Motor_Run = 0 after the
      transition (OTE cleared at prescan) and does not restart until START is pressed. Confirm the force table is empty and
      save the final project.
 NOTE
 Where bench switches are not available, inputs may be simulated by forcing on the bench controller only, and all forces are
 cleared at the end of the lab. Verify on bench before field use.

Expected Results: Motor_Run energizes on START, holds through the seal-in, and drops on STOP, overload, E-stop, a
broken stop wire, or a Program-to-Run transition. It restarts only on a new START. No forces remain at the end of the lab.
Review Questions: Appendix F.2, Lab 3.
Lab 4: Configure and Tune a PID Loop
Objective: Configure a PID instruction in a periodic task, simulate a first-order-plus-dead-time process, tune it with the Ziegler-
Nichols closed-loop method, and verify bumpless transfer to manual.
Equipment / Tools: Studio 5000 v36 with the bench controller or Logix Emulate; trending (Studio 5000 trend or plant
historian); laptop.
Safety Precautions: Use a simulated process only; do not connect the PID output to live process equipment. Disable all
external outputs during this exercise.
Background Theory: Proportional action responds to the current error; integral action eliminates steady-state offset;
derivative action responds to the rate of change. Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop tuning uses the ultimate gain (Ku), the gain at
which the loop sustains a steady oscillation, and the period of that oscillation (Tu) to calculate starting tuning values. The Logix
PID requires a fixed execution interval, so it is placed in a periodic task with .UPD equal to the task period.
Procedure
 1. Create a periodic task "PID_Task" with a period of 100 ms and a program "PID_Lab". Create tags: PV_Sim (REAL),
      CV_Sim (REAL), CV_Delay (REAL[20]), i (DINT), and PIC_LAB (PID).
 2. Create a Structured Text routine "Process_Sim" with the code below. The 20-element array at 100 ms gives 2 s of dead
      time; the last line is a first-order lag with gain 1 and a time constant of about 2 s.
 (* Process_Sim — first-order-plus-dead-time simulator, 100 ms periodic task *)
 FOR i := 19 TO 1 BY -1 DO
     CV_Delay[i] := CV_Delay[i-1];
 END_FOR;
 CV_Delay[0] := CV_Sim;
 PV_Sim := PV_Sim + (CV_Delay[19] - PV_Sim) * 0.05;

 3. Create a ladder routine "PID_Logic" with the rungs below and set the main routine to call Process_Sim and then
      PID_Logic. The PID rung is unconditional.

Rung 0 – Output tracking (bumpless entry to manual)
 XIO(PIC_LAB.SWM)MOVE(PIC_LAB.OUT,PIC_LAB.SO);
 Rung 1 – PID (unconditional)
 PID(PIC_LAB,PV_Sim,0,CV_Sim,0,0,0);

 4. Configure PIC_LAB: .UPD = 0.1; .PE = 0 (independent gains); .MAXI/.MINI = 100.0/0.0; .MAXS/.MINS =
      100.0/0.0; .MAXO/.MINO = 100.0/0.0; .CA = 0 (reverse acting, E = SP − PV, because a higher CV raises PV); .SP =
      50.0; .KP = 0.1; .KI = 0.0; .KD = 0.0; .SWM = 0 (auto).
 5. Download and run. Observe PV_Sim settle near 50 with proportional action only (offset remains).
 6. Find the ultimate gain (Ku): with .KI = 0 and .KD = 0, increase .KP in steps (0.5, 1.0, 2.0 …) until PV_Sim sustains a
      steady oscillation (neither growing nor decaying). Record Ku.
 7. Measure the ultimate period (Tu) in seconds from the trend. Record Tu.
 8. Calculate Ziegler-Nichols PI values: Kc = 0.45 × Ku; Ti = Tu / 1.2 (seconds). With .PE = 0: .KP = Kc and .KI = Kc / Ti (1/s).
      With .PE = 1: .KP = Kc and .KI = Ti in minutes per repeat (Ti / 60). Leave .KD = 0.
 9. Enter the values. Step .SP from 50 to 70 and observe settling time, overshoot, and offset.
 10. Adjust: if oscillatory, reduce .KP by 20%; if slow, increase integral action by 10%.
 11. Bumpless transfer test: set .SWM = 1. The output holds at the last automatic value (.SO tracked .OUT). Change .SO by
      10% and observe PV. Set .SWM = 0 and confirm the output resumes smoothly from the manual value.
 12. Record the final tuning values and trend a setpoint step showing PV tracking.
Expected Results: PV tracks SP with less than about 20% overshoot and settles within a few oscillation periods. Steady-state
offset is zero (integral action). Entering manual holds the output without a bump, and returning to auto resumes smoothly.
Review Questions: Appendix F.2, Lab 4.

Lab 7: MSG Read — Inter-PLC Communication
Objective: Configure a MSG instruction to read a REAL tag from a peer controller over EtherNet/IP with periodic polling, stale-
data detection, and error capture, and verify the behavior on a cable pull.
Equipment / Tools: Two bench controllers (1769-L33ER at v36) on the same Ethernet network, Studio 5000, laptop.
Safety Precautions: Bench controllers only. Confirm IP addresses do not conflict with the production network. Do not perform
this lab on a production system without engineering authorization.

Background Theory: Explicit MSG instructions allow a ControlLogix controller to read from or write to tags in another
controller on demand. This is used extensively in gas plants to exchange data between the main process PLC and compressor
package OEM PLCs, metering computers, and analyzer systems.
Procedure
 1. On the target controller (Controller B, example IP 192.168.1.30), create a controller-scoped REAL tag
      "Comp_Speed_Fdbk" with External Access = Read Only (or Read/Write). Set its value to 1800.0.
 2. On the source controller (Controller A), add Controller B to the I/O configuration under the Ethernet port so that the
      message path can be browsed.
 3. In Controller A, create tags: Comp_MSG_Read (MESSAGE), Comp_Speed_Remote (REAL), Comp_Speed (REAL),
      Comp_MSG_Poll and Comp_MSG_Stale (TIMER), Comp_Comms_Fault (BOOL), Comp_MSG_ErrCode and
      Comp_MSG_ExtErr (DINT).
 4. Configure Comp_MSG_Read: Message Type = CIP Data Table Read; Source Element = Comp_Speed_Fdbk; Number of

Lab 8: BPCS Trip String and Time-Limited Bypass (Not SIS / Not ESD SIF)

 WARNING — BPCS Training Logic
 This is BPCS training logic. The output is not an ESD final element, and this bypass pattern is never copied into a SIS. A
 production SIF bypass requires a bypass permit, safety-engineer approval, a time limit, and an operator display, and is
 outside the technician authorization envelope (Section 0.2).

Objective: On a training controller only, build a BPCS trip string with PAHH, LAHH, and manual trip inputs; add a
maintenance bypass with key-switch authorization and a self-expiring timer; and document the bypass as a note on a training
C&E worksheet. This lab does not authorize SIS work.
Equipment / Tools: Studio 5000, bench controller with bench DI switches (NC trip inputs and a key switch), laptop, C&E
matrix template (Section 9.4).

Safety Precautions: Training controller only. Use a short bypass duration for training (5 minutes). In production, every BPCS
trip bypass requires written authorization (bypass permit), a time limit, an active operator notification, and removal immediately
on completion of the maintenance task. SIS bypasses follow the plant functional-safety procedure.
Background Theory: BPCS trip bypasses are sometimes used for testing process interlocks. SIS/SIF bypasses are a
different, higher-authority activity and are not performed in this lab. A bypassed trip leaves the process with less protection.
Best practice requires (1) authorization, (2) a time-limited bypass that expires automatically, (3) a continuous alarm informing
operators that the trip is bypassed, and (4) increased operator vigilance during the bypass period.
Procedure
 1. Create a program "BPCS_Trip_Lab". Create tags: SEP_PAHH_OK, SEP_LAHH_OK, MAN_TRIP_OK (BOOL aliases to
      bench NC switches, 1 = healthy); BYP_KEY (BOOL alias to the bench key switch); SEP_Byp (UDT with members TON
      (TIMER), Expired, Sup_Reset, Alm (BOOL)); SEP_Lab_Causes_OK, SEP_Trip_OK, SEP_Trip_Alm (BOOL);
      Area.HMI_Reset, Area.Reset_ONS, Area.Reset_Pulse (BOOL).
 2. Enter the rungs below (Pattern A1 reset pulse, bypass timer, trip string, and the Snippet 6 latch and reset).

 Rung 1 – Clear HMI reset request

 Rung 3 – Expiry latch

 Rung 5 – Clear supervisor reset request
 XIC(SEP_Byp.Sup_Reset)OTU(SEP_Byp.Sup_Reset);
 Rung 6 – Trip causes (PAHH bypassed only while timing)

Lab 9: Network Troubleshooting — Find a Lost FLEX I/O Node
Objective: Simulate a FLEX I/O adapter communication loss, use systematic diagnostics (RSLinx browsing, ping, Studio 5000
I/O diagnostics, LED status) to identify and restore the lost node. Document RPI considerations.

Equipment / Tools: Studio 5000, RSLinx Classic or FactoryTalk Linx, training FLEX I/O bank (1794-AENTR), Ethernet
network switch, laptop with command prompt access.
Safety Precautions: Training equipment only. On a production system, any deliberate disconnection of a FLEX I/O bank
causes loss of that I/O — notify operator and get authorization before any network cable manipulation.
Background Theory: EtherNet/IP uses a keep-alive mechanism: if the controller does not receive an I/O update from the
adapter within a defined connection timeout period, it declares a connection fault. The timeout is typically 4× the RPI value.
Understanding LED status codes is faster than launching software diagnostics in an emergency.
Procedure
 1. Start with the FLEX bank fully operational and all modules showing green in Studio 5000. Record the normal LED states
      on the 1794-AENTR: MS (Module Status) = solid green; NS (Network Status) = solid green (connection established).
 2. Disconnect the Ethernet cable from the 1794-AENTR adapter. Start a stopwatch.
 3. In Studio 5000 (online), observe the I/O tree and note when the adapter shows a fault. The controller declares the
      connection fault after about 4 × RPI; the software display may take longer to refresh.
 4. Observe the AENTR adapter LEDs: MS remains solid green (module powered and healthy); NS flashes red (connection
      timeout).
 NOTE
 AENTR NS LED behavior on connection timeout. Verify on bench before field use.

 5. At the Windows command prompt: ping 192.168.1.20 (training adapter IP). Observe "Request timed out" — no response
      confirms adapter is unreachable.
 6. Open RSLinx Classic → Communications → RSWho (Who Active). Browse the EtherNet/IP driver — the adapter should
      not appear in the browse tree (confirms network-level disconnection).
 7. Physically check the cable: inspect both ends (adapter port and switch port) for a seated RJ-45 connector. Check switch
      port LED — if no LED, port is not detecting link.
 8. Reconnect the Ethernet cable. Observe switch port LED lights up (link established).
 9. At command prompt: ping 192.168.1.20 -n 10. Confirm all 10 packets receive replies with low latency (<5 ms).
 10. In Studio 5000, observe I/O tree — adapter recovers automatically. Record recovery time.
 11. RS Who Browse — confirm adapter reappears. All modules show green status.
 12. Experiment with RPI: change the adapter RPI to 5 ms. Disconnect the cable again; the connection timeout is now about
      20 ms. Reconnect and change the RPI back to 20 ms. Trade-off: lower RPI gives faster fault detection but higher network
      load.
 13. Document findings: fault detection time at 20 ms RPI, recovery time, LED state descriptions.
Expected Results: Connection fault declared after about 4 × RPI (≈ 80 ms at 20 ms RPI); the I/O tree display may lag.
Recovery is automatic on cable reconnection. All previous I/O states are restored. LED diagnostics identify the fault before
software tools.

Lab 10: Alarm Rationalization Workshop
Objective: Apply ISA-18.2 alarm rationalization methodology to 10 existing HMI alarms, fill out rationalization worksheets,
reassign priorities, adjust setpoints and deadbands, and document changes.
Equipment / Tools: ISA-18.2 standard (or facility alarm philosophy document), alarm rationalization worksheet template
(Section 6.3), HMI alarm history data (30-day period), laptop.
Safety Precautions: All setpoint changes must be reviewed and approved by the process engineer before implementation.
Do not change alarm setpoints on a production system without MOC authorization.
Background Theory: ISA-18.2 requires that every alarm be individually rationalized — meaning the cause, consequence,
operator response, priority, setpoint, and deadband are documented and justified. The goal is to ensure alarms demand
operator action, are unique and meaningful, and do not overwhelm the operator during upset conditions.
Procedure
 1. Review the 30-day alarm history report. Identify the top 10 most frequent alarms (bad actors).
 2. For each alarm, fill out the rationalization worksheet (Section 6.3 template): Tag, Description, Cause, Consequence,
      Existing Safeguards, Proposed Priority (1–4), Proposed Setpoint, Proposed Deadband, Required Operator Action.
 3. For each alarm, determine if it meets the ISA-18.2 definition of a true alarm: "An audible and/or visible means of indicating
      to the operator an equipment malfunction, process deviation, or abnormal condition requiring a timely response."
 4. Identify any alarms that are NOT true alarms (e.g., informational only, status flags, equipment position feedback).
      Recommend removal or reclassification as "advisory" (no sound, no operator action required).

5. Identify any chattering alarms (activating more than once per 10 minutes over the 30-day period). For each: increase
      deadband, add time delay, or move setpoint further from normal operating point.
 6. Assign ISA-18.2 priority to each alarm: Critical (1), High (2), Medium (3), Low (4). Justify each assignment based on
      consequence severity and required response time.
 7. Document setpoint rationalization: compare existing setpoint to normal operating range. Ensure adequate margin between
      normal operation and alarm setpoint to avoid nuisance alarms during normal transients.
 8. Present the 10 rationalized alarms in a completed worksheet table.
 9. Identify any alarms that should be state-based (active only in certain operating modes, e.g., active only when compressor
      is running).
 10. Write a brief summary report: total alarms reviewed, number reclassified, priority changes, setpoint changes, expected
      reduction in alarm rate.
Expected Results: All 10 alarms have completed rationalization worksheets. At least 2–3 alarms are reclassified or have
adjusted setpoints/deadbands. Summary report estimates projected alarm rate reduction.

PID Tuning Rules of Thumb
  • Start conservatively: begin with Kc = 0.5, integral and derivative off. Increase Kc until the loop responds without
     oscillation before adding integral action.
  • Integral eliminates offset: Add Ki gradually to remove steady-state error. Too much Ki → oscillation and windup.
  • Derivative on noise: Avoid Kd for noisy pressure signals. Use only on slow, smooth processes (temperature) and only if
     loop is stable with P+I first.
  • Ziegler-Nichols (closed loop): PI: Kc = 0.45 × Ku, Ti = Tu / 1.2. PID: Kc = 0.6 × Ku, Ti = Tu / 2, Td = Tu / 8. Ti and Td are
     in the time units of Tu; convert to the PID form in use (Appendix B).
  • If oscillating: reduce Kc by 20% first. If slow with offset: increase integral action by 10%. Kc and integral action are not
     adjusted at the same time.

Appendix B: Useful Formulas

4–20 mA to Engineering Units (Forward and Reverse)

 (* FORWARD: mA signal → engineering units *)
 EU  = EU_Min + ((mA - 4.0) / 16.0) * (EU_Max - EU_Min);

 (* REVERSE: engineering units → expected mA *)
 mA  = ((EU - EU_Min) / (EU_Max - EU_Min)) * 16.0 + 4.0;

 (* Percent of span *)
 Pct = (mA - 4.0) / 16.0 * 100.0;

Raw Counts to Engineering Units (1794-IE8 and 1756-IF8)

 (* 1794-IE8 FLEX I/O, 4-20 mA mode: 0 counts = 4 mA, 30840 counts = 20 mA *)
 EU = EU_Min + (DINT_TO_REAL(Raw_Counts) / 30840.0) * (EU_Max - EU_Min);
 (* Example: Raw = 15420 (12 mA), range 0-300 PSIG → EU = 150.0 PSIG *)

 (* 1756-IF8: use float (engineering units) data format with module     *)
 (* scaling (Low/High Signal 4.0/20.0 mA → Low/High EU) and read the     *)
 (* channel data directly. In integer mode 4 mA reads about -20030       *)
 (* counts; scale from the module manual, not from 0-32767.              *)

 NOTE
 IE8 count values from the 1794 analog user manual; IF8 integer-mode counts depend on module configuration. Verify on
 bench before field use.

Orifice Plate Flow Calculation (Differential Pressure)

 (* AGA-3 / ISO 5167 simplified — reference only; custody transfer uses the flow computer *)
 Q_actual = Cd * (PI/4) * d^2 * SQRT(2 * dP / rho)

   Q_actual = volumetric flow rate (m3/s or ft3/s)
   Cd       = discharge coefficient (about 0.6 for a sharp-edged orifice; per AGA/ISO)
   d        = orifice bore diameter (m or ft)
   dP       = differential pressure across the orifice (Pa or lbf/ft2)
   rho      = fluid density at flowing conditions (kg/m3 or lbm/ft3)

 (* For gas: rho = MW * P / (Z * R * T)                                   *)
 (*   MW = molecular weight; P = absolute pressure; Z = compressibility;   *)
 (*   R = gas constant; T = absolute temperature                          *)

 (* In Logix (v36 name SQRT, legacy SQR): *)
 IF DP_Value < 0.0 THEN DP_Value := 0.0; END_IF;     (* no MAX function in Logix ST *)
 Q_flow := K * SQRT(DP_Value);

 NOTE
 DP_Value is a copy of DP_Transmitter.Value. K is a calibration constant from the flow element data sheet.

PID Output Formula (Independent Form, .PE = 0)

 (* Independent PID form — each term acts on the error *)
 E(t)   = SP - PV                 (* .CA = 0, reverse acting; .CA = 1 uses PV - SP *)

 OUT(t) = Kp * E(t)
        + Ki * integral(E dt)     (* integral — eliminates offset; Ki in 1/s *)
        + Kd * dE/dt              (* derivative — responds to rate; Kd in s  *)

 (* Discrete form, sampled at Ts = .UPD: *)
 OUT_n  = Kp * E_n
        + Ki * Ts * sum(E)
        + Kd * (E_n - E_n-1) / Ts

 (* Output clamped: .MINO <= OUT <= .MAXO; integral stops accumulating while clamped *)

Ziegler-Nichols Tuning Formulas (Closed Loop)
 Controller type                          Kc                               Ti (integral time)                       Td (derivative time)
 P only                                   0.5 × Ku                         ∞ (no integral)                          0 (no derivative)
 PI                                       0.45 × Ku                        Tu / 1.2                                 0 (no derivative)
 PID (classic)                            0.6 × Ku                         Tu / 2                                   Tu / 8
 PID (some overshoot)                     0.33 × Ku                        Tu / 2                                   Tu / 3

Ku = ultimate gain — the proportional gain at which the loop sustains a steady oscillation with integral and derivative off. Tu =
period of that oscillation. Ti and Td are in the time units of Tu. Logix PID conversion: with .PE = 0 (independent), KP = Kc, KI =
Kc / Ti (1/s, Ti in seconds), KD = Kc × Td (s). With .PE = 1 (dependent), KP = Kc, KI = Ti (minutes per repeat), KD = Td
(minutes).
